analysis.one_liner: Bans federal agencies from buying genetic-sequencing equipment or services from foreign-adversary-linked biotech companies.
analysis.headline: The bill won unanimous bipartisan approval in a Senate committee and was placed on the Senate's calendar of pending business, but the full Senate never voted on it before the Congress ended in January 2025.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would stop federal agencies from buying biotech equipment or services — things like DNA sequencers and gene-testing services — from a list of companies tied to foreign adversaries, starting with the Chinese-linked firms BGI, MGI, Complete Genomics, and WuXi AppTec. It would also stop federal grant and loan money from being spent on those companies' products, and it directs intelligence agencies to report on the risk that Americans' genetic data collected abroad could be used against U.S. security interests. The goal is to keep Americans' genetic information out of the hands of foreign governments through federal contracting.
analysis.who_benefits: Federal employees, service members, and people whose genetic data passes through federal health and research programs gain a legal barrier against that data reaching foreign adversary governments through federal purchases. U.S.-based biotech equipment and genomics companies also gain, because federal agencies and grant recipients would have to buy from suppliers not on the concern list.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Federal workers, service members, and U.S. genomics firms

how_it_helps.text: Prohibits executive agencies from procuring biotechnology equipment or services from 'biotechnology companies of concern' — including BGI, MGI, Complete Genomics, WuXi AppTec, and their subsidiaries and successors — or from entering contracts that require their use.
Bars agencies from obligating or expending loan or grant funds on those companies' equipment or services, so federal research money cannot flow to them either.

Requires the Director of National Intelligence to assess, and report to Congress on, the national security risk posed by Americans' genetic and related biological data (genomic, proteomic, and similar 'multiomic' data) collected or stored by a foreign adversary.
Directs the Office of Management and Budget to build and at least annually update the list of companies of concern, and to review any company's designation after it submits opposing information.

analysis.who_pays: The named Chinese-linked companies and their U.S. customers — federal contractors, universities, and labs that receive federal grants — would have to replace existing equipment and services with alternatives, which typically costs more and disrupts ongoing research. Taxpayers could bear some of that through higher federal procurement costs. The bill authorizes no additional funds for carrying out its own requirements.
analysis.who_pays_short: Chinese-linked biotech firms and federal grant recipients

drawbacks.text: The ban extends to loan and grant recipients, so universities and research labs using federal money would have to swap out sequencers and services mid-project, and the bill authorizes no additional funding to cover the switch.

The bill covers only federal contracting — it does not stop private hospitals, insurers, or consumer genetics companies from using the same firms' equipment or services, so most Americans' genetic data is only partially protected.

Agencies can waive the ban case-by-case with White House budget office approval, and designations under the catch-all criteria (rather than the four named companies) are not made public until a final determination, which limits transparency about who is covered and why.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The security rationale is straightforward: genetic data is a permanent identifier that foreign governments could use for surveillance or targeting, and federal money should not buy tools that can harvest it. The main honest cost is disruption — researchers and contractors losing access to cheaper Chinese-supplied sequencing and having to requalify alternatives, with no new money to ease the transition — and the protection is incomplete because it stops at federal contracting. The compliance and cost burden on grant-funded labs is real but modest compared with the data-protection goal.

outcome.mechanism: The Senate's Homeland Security committee approved the bill unanimously and it sat on the Senate's official calendar of pending business for over three months, but the full Senate never voted on it before the Congress ended on January 3, 2025.

narrative.text: Senator Gary Peters, a Democrat, introduced the bill in December 2023 with ten cosponsors from both parties — nine Republicans and one Democrat.
The Senate Homeland Security and Governmental Affairs Committee ordered the bill reported favorably with an amendment in March 2024 and formally reported it on September 23, 2024.
The reported version was placed on the Senate Legislative Calendar under General Orders (Calendar No. 521) on September 23, 2024 — the holding pen for bills awaiting floor action.
No floor vote ever occurred, and the bill died when the 118th Congress ended on January 3, 2025.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Because the bill never became law, the named companies keep their access to U.S. federal business, federal agencies and grant recipients avoid the compliance costs of switching suppliers, and U.S. genomics firms did not gain the protected market the bill would have handed them. The Americans whose genetic data the bill aimed to shield got no new protection.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Chinese-linked biotech firms and their U.S. customers

for.name: Gary Peters
for.role: U.S. Senator (D-MI); bill sponsor and chair of the Homeland Security and Governmental Affairs Committee
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill, chaired the committee that approved it, and reported it to the Senate floor with an amendment in the nature of a substitute.

for.role: Senate Republican cosponsors (Hagerty, Romney, Marshall, Lankford, Scott, Hawley, Rubio, Britt, Hoeven)
for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill at introduction, giving it bipartisan backing.

for.name: Senate Homeland Security and Governmental Affairs Committee
for.what_they_did: Ordered the bill reported favorably with a substitute amendment in March 2024 and formally reported it in September 2024.

against.name: Chuck Schumer
against.what_they_did: Never scheduled the bill for a floor vote after it sat on the Senate calendar from September 23, 2024 until the Congress ended.

sides.party_line_note: Sponsorship split evenly across party lines — one Democrat sponsor joined by one Democratic and nine Republican cosponsors — and the committee reported it favorably with no recorded opposition.

industries.industry: Chinese-linked genomics and biotech firms (BGI, MGI, Complete Genomics, WuXi AppTec and subsidiaries)
industries.note: The bill would cut them off from federal contracts and federal grant-funded purchases outright. Their business model depends on selling sequencing equipment and services into U.S. markets, including government channels where Americans' genetic data is processed.

industries.industry: U.S. biotech equipment and genomics suppliers
industries.note: Federal agencies and grant recipients would have to buy sequencers and related services from suppliers not on the concern list, effectively handing domestic firms a protected federal market. Their gain coincides with the public's interest in keeping genetic data away from foreign adversaries, though the entrenchment also means less price competition for federal buyers.

industries.industry: Universities, research labs, and federal contractors
industries.note: These institutions would have to replace equipment and services bought with federal funds on a fixed timeline, with no new money authorized for the transition. Some are the very institutions whose federal research the bill is meant to protect.
